projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Albert H. Zimmerman was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mr. Zimmerman is a World War II Veteran. Mr. Zimmerman served in the U.S. Army, his highest rank was master sergeant. I'm Tom Swope. This interview was recorded at Mr. Zimmerman's home in Bedford Heights, Ohio on June 29th, 2004. Albert was 82 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Well, I was born and raised here in Cleveland, Ohio, so in 1941 I was with my dad at 933 Ansell (ph) Road in Cleveland, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you in 1941? When were you born?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: I was born April 11, 1922.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were 19?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: I had just graduated from East High School. I was interviewed by my only employer for my entire life, Dunn and Bradstreet. They talked to us, and I thought, ah, that's what I'm going to do. I'm going to start there as a messenger boy and see if I can work my way up. They treated me very well. I ended up as district service manager. I worked for them for 33 years, took early retirement in 1983 because my wife was ill, and it was just fine. When we talk about my wife, she too attended East High School, graduated from East High, and we were married. I was inducted into the service in 1942.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before we get to that, do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: December 7th, 1941.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Pearl Harbor day?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Yes. I was a radio operator, amateur radio operator. My call was W8 uniform Yankee, November, W8UIN, and that night I was on radio, and I don't remember who I was talking to, a local man, and everything was interrupted when December 7th occurred. And both of us were of draft age, and we said, "Well, it's not going to be too long now before we'd be going in," and he said, "no, Rocky." By the way, that's the name, Rocky is used, Rocky, within conjunction with amateur radio. Most of the guys know me as Rocky. He said, "I'm way ahead of you. I knew this was coming, so I already enlisted, and I'll be going in very soon." Little did I know that the numbers would be called and I would be inducted as well, but I was inducted. I did not volunteer.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So then why did you go again?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Actually, I went in August of 1942, and I think I went to Columbus. I don't recall this, but I think I went to Columbus, and then from there I went to Fort Eustis, Virginia. That's where I took my first basic training.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you recall your first basic training?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Yep, that regimen was really something, because I lived and I was carefree; but boy, at Fort Eustis, you snap to. You did what was told, you were told, and there were consequences if you didn't. So this was an entirely new life to me, but I put up with it, and I was fine. Completing Fort Eustis, I was then sent, because of my radio experience, back to Camp Davis, North Carolina where I went to radio school. After graduating, or after completing my course at radio school, I then became immediately Cadre for the 12th -- that's 1, 2, 12888 Group, anti-aircraft group, and we were activated at North Carolina, and new draftees were coming in, so we were the Cadre, and we had to give them their basic training. And after completing basic training then we went into maneuvers, so I had North Carolina maneuvers, Louisiana maneuvers, maneuvers galore.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any stories come to light about any of those?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Well, yes. Again, as with Dunn and Bradstreet, I was promoted from messenger boy to file clerk, to a telephone operator, to a reporter, and so forth. But when I say a reporter, I wrote reports on the businesses, and the same thing happened at 12888 Group, I started there as a corporal T-5, and before I knew it, I was a sergeant. And then before I knew it, I was a staff sergeant, and it continued on until I became the communications chief, so I was three up, and three down in a master sergeant, and this was all done during the course of our maneuvers in the United States. I terminated at Camp Polk, Louisiana. I forget exactly where when we were also diverted to a fire, force fire that occurred not too far from Louisiana north, but I don't remember how far. And then this was suddenly stopped, and a colonel, my CO, my commanding officer was Colonel Bailey, West Point graduate. I respected Colonel Bailey throughout the entire war, a fine -- very, very fine man. Anyway, it was terminated, and we were told to report back to one Fort Camp Davis, and off to New York, New York. We boarded a ship that came from -- it was -- can we stop it for a minute?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: We boarded a ship that was the Duchess of Richmond that had come in from Australia, and it was -- we didn't know where we were going. We didn't know whether it was Italy or where, but later on we found out. Colonel Bailey had a short meeting with the officers, and because I was in communications I was included in the elite, so-called, affair, and we knew we were now heading for England. We picked up a convoy somewhere in the Atlantic. And to make a long story short, we docked at East Liverpool.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before we get to that, do you remember about when that cross was?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Yes. It was on Christmas of 1943. We were very close to England, so we celebrated Christmas aboard ship, and then from there we docked at East Liverpool, and then went down to South Hampton. The Salsbury planes -- that's the word. The Salsbury planes. That's where most of the men coming in from the states were going, and setting up operations for the eventual crossing of the channel and going into France. We were very busy with fake messages. We were told by our officers that we were to just saturate the air waves with messages of all kinds to confuse the Germans. They were supposedly thinking we were going to land at point A, and everything pointed to this point A, which was Kelly, and we did not -- I mean, we -- various places. And this continued on until June about, and in June we knew that we were going, and other things had to be waterproofed. Cars had to be waterproofed. All of our equipment was double checked and so fort, and the date --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any idea where the actual landing would be?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Not at this time, no. No. It wasn't actually until, I would say, five days before we were to get on the LST, which would take us to France that I knew where at the point it was then Normandie, and it was D-Day. Omaha Beach was the beach that we would land on. We were nervous. No combat experience, none, and all I can say is, we prayed a lot, and we took things as they came. We were trained. We knew this was not going to be a joyride, and we were going to do the best that we could. They gave us -- not me. I was lucky. I was not seasick. I remember Dordella (ph), who was, I think he was a corporal, maybe a sergeant, the radio operator; but, oh, he just dreaded the water, and on the ship going over to England he was just sick all the time. He was at the rail always, and he was worried about crossing the channel disgracing himself and the rest. So several of the boys gave him their sleeping pills, and he was out like a light. He was out like a light. He took so many. Anyway, we couldn't get in on D-Day. We just couldn't. There was no way. We stayed on board the ship. It was an LST, by the way, and the original on top of a thing to prevent low fighting planes from harming us. The time came for the landing by us just D plus two when we came in, and we got into -- it was very nice. It was a limey that drove the ship in, and then he did real well because we got into no more than two feet of water, but on our port side the LST, two of them on our port side were hit with shells coming in from the mountains -- not the mountains, the hills, the gun in placements, and then the rat came down, and we drove off. The engineers had already put tape so that we were not hit by mines, and we took the tape and got up to higher ground. And just to show you how naive we were, we dug holes. We put up a tent thinking this shrapnel would bounce off the tent. Oh, it was -- it was a comedy of errors, but thank the Lord nothing like this happened, and we were far enough behind the lines that we heard fire, but we never saw a German. No one came close, and it was a relatively restful evening.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So still kind of a mess when you first landed?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Omaha was a mess. Oh, yes, absolutely. That's why I say this tape that the engineers had put down certainly prevented us from riding into mines. Now, we knew that we were hidden in the battle itself, and the training that we had received it was good, and this helped. I mean, immediately we had outposts. You see, you have to remember, we are communications, so we had to make communications for our headquarters which was 12888 Group to battery. That's where all the officers were. The CO was, of course, Pearl Bailey, and we had Colonel Schrekinger (ph), and many majors, and things and so forth. And we had battalions, ouffers, 40 millimeters and 90 millimeters, automatic weapons which were used for supporting infantry, so I had to have a crew that was good as far as laying wire. I also had to have good operators, radio operators, and we were communicating back in England with 19th Corps because we were part of a 19th Corps First Army, and we stayed with them until around Ahken. That's when we were switched to another corp. But the boys -- and I give all of them credit. We've had reunions quite a few, and I still respect them, and they respected me. They all refer to me as Sarg. And it was nice, it was. I respected them, and they respected me. We did a lot of things together, a lot of things. We saw a lot of things, and it was just a good group, a good group. As far as the first -- well, I'm going to say five days, the first five days, we were naive. We were -- I've got to tell one story. Perkins, Orville Perkins, sergeant, he swore the duffle bag moved, and we -- it was about 2:00 in the morning. We heard a repeated fire of his rifle, and boy, we thought we were attacked. We really did. We all got out and we had our holes, and we were set to do anything that we could to hold our positions. And Perkins was the one that said, "I shot at my own duffle bag." And we all look at him and wouldn't believe him. And, yes, he told us that it moved, and that's why he shot it. I mean, now, it doesn't sound like anything, but at that particular time, believe me, it meant something. Then Bedcheck Charley came over several times. We accommodated the skies, of course, but not completely, and so these would come over, and that's when it was important to have that guy, and it was important to have hold fire in effect because there were night fighters, and when they were up, you were -- when you shot up there, you didn't know if you were hitting a Gerry or hitting your own, or the Likens, or the British. So hold fire was very important as far as communication was concerned. Now, you're talking radio, not telephones.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Hold fire was simply the hold fire to get to the guns?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Yes. Hold fire would be the command that would be given by the officers through the radio operator who then said to the 130 battalion, "Hold fire is in effect," and that meant that. I mean, it meant that, and if you didn't, why you would have problems. To me, I was very glad to get home. The Lord was good to me. I'll say that because there were situations that came up where I -- for example, now, this is farther on down in Germany in France. Let's say Fort Germany. We were tired. We had laid, I don't know, maybe 30 miles of wire, that's W110B, and the guys were tired. We got to a -- actually, it was a bombed out residence, maybe. I don't know. It was a house or a barn or whatnot, anymore, but it had shelter, and I sat down. This looks like it's pretty good. Why don't we stay here. And boy, they agreed right away. And now, they went with the equipment. You rested. You rested when you could because many times you just couldn't rest. And I walked into the area after it had been secured by the boys, so to speak, and low and behold, I don't know how to put this. It was misty, and I swear this was in English that I heard a voice saying, "Don't stay here." And I looked, and I looked, and I couldn't see anyone, and yet that, "Don't stay here" was in me, and I just took it, and ran. I said, "Boys, -- I used different words. Let's go," and they kept saying, "Sergeant, What's wrong with you? What do you mean? This is fine. We're going to stay here." And I had said, "I'm your sergeant. I'm telling you to get your stuff together. We're going." And we moved, oh, maybe -- maybe a mile and a half down the road, and we stayed at a place that wasn't near as nice, but we stayed there. And the following -- oh, that's right. They didn't take all of the wires. Some of the wire was left. There were rolls of the wire. I sent him back, that was Swank. Swank is the sergeant, the wire crew. I sent him back, and he came back and he says, "Sergeant, we would have been killed, all of us." The Germans had the sites on the particular place that we were going to stay, and it was just wired out. The wires all gone. We have to go to the depot and get some more wire. I'll do that. I just thank Him for saying, "Don't stay here." I mean, I remember that since the day of, and the guys -- the guys did too. We had close encounters, let's say, but it was good. I just lost one man, that was Chief Cottrell. Cottrell was an Ohio boy, and he was on a pole, lame wire, and a sniper got him in the back of the head, and I had 23 men, some were wounded, yeah. I was lucky. I did not get wounded, but some were wounded, and no one killed except Chief, and I dedicated to him and the memories of 12888 Group is the first page. I can only say that the United States has a purpose in this world, and I think the purpose is to help other countries, and I think also the purpose is to set an example of what really can be done when you have a company or a country that believes in what's right is right, and the wrong should be punished. I am a Christian and always have been active. I know one of the things that I told God after I hit the beach and I was all right, and I got to -- I can't even think of the name, the little town right at the top of the hill. I got pictures of it. That if it is the Lord's will, then I will do my best to be a Sunday school teacher when I got back and do anything that I could to help peace continue throughout the world. And the Lord answered my prayer. And truthfully, I was a Sunday school teacher for 40 years. The library at the church is named after me, and I'm very proud of that. Enough on that. That was rough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before you got to Ahken, do you remember anything else about the Normandie that comes to mind?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. We moved fast. See, the Germans were retreated, and they wanted -- they, I'm talking about supreme command. They wanted to cut off the Germans, and I forget how many armies were involved, and so we were involved in keeping communications with the various battalions to make this possible. They over extended us. As I said, we had 23 men, and you could just do so much, and these guys were working day and night, and we did. We kept everyone in communication with one another, and later on citations were given to the 12th group. That's communications for the communications that we're intact and used, and it was good. It was good, so this all took place -- you had your marginal line first which we had to take care of because it was being operated by the Germans. Your marginal line, then you have your Sigrid line. And as I said, before getting to Ahken. We had close combat. I mean, these guys were terrific. I mean, I don't care if it was the radio crew or the wiremen or the messenger boys, or the switchboard operators. I name them all. They were good. They knew how to fire the rifle. They did a good job. They did a good job, and we all benefited. We all benefited. And communication, I can only reiterate is so vital and so important because without communications you just don't get things done. And they had their lives that were given to making this communication possible. And it was just good ones, good guys. That's about all I can say on that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So okay. So where was Ahken? Was that --

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: That was in 1944.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What, October, November?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Around October, yes. Yes, because now the 19th Corps was involved in it, but for some reason the 12th group was changed. See, the 12888 Group had all of the anti-aircraft, all the anti-aircraft because now by the time of Ahken the airwaves weren't covered by us, period. I had very few planes that would get in. Oh, some did, but I mean, very few. Instead of us being anti-aircraft, we are now self-supporting infantry and tanks. I mean, a tank with the 40s and 90s boom. We helped the 12th Corps, and I know we were directly under -- I forget the general's name. I'm guessing at that. And he wanted us to help support the German counter-attack which was being planned by the tanks, and so now what Colonel Bailey did was put our positions as far as positions -- as far as the battalions are concerned, with guns in different positions than any aircraft. They were now against the tanks and certain codes that we used for planes could not be used for tanks because they would mean certain things. I mean, you see them, and you knew what to do, so we had to come up with a different SOP, standard operating procedure, so I was enlisted to come up with a new SOP for the use of the addax against the tanks. And Colonel Bailey had three officers, Riley, Major Riley, which was -- he was terrific, Captain Baker, and Lieutenant Taskey (ph), and they were the officers that formed the new SOP. And then it was entrusted to me to get to all of the outfits that were under us, and I say Ahken was taken, and -- oh, that's right. We now we get something personal. After we got into Belgium, I met an underground, the name was Walters, W-A-L-T-E-R-S. I have pictures of him. He was underground for a band, and he definitely helped us in locating certain areas that were free for communication and the rest. Now, he's from her H, double E, R-L-E-N, Heerlen, Holland, not too far from Austria or the Albert Canal. I met his wife. He did not last during the war. He was killed by Germans in Holland, and I don't know exactly where, but he was killed; his wife was also killed by planes, British planes that dropped bombs too soon, but the Holland people were killed that way. He and the wife had a little daughter, and I almost adopted her. She was close to me. All of my rations, anything that I could spare I would give to them for the little girl, so there's a very soft spot in my heart for the Holland because of what's happened. I mean, I just wanted her. Colonel Bailey had the papers that were going to be approved for me to start adoption proceedings, but then the Bulge took place, and we were gone, and then we were shut down to Liege, and we had to do our best as far as the Bulge. And I might as well say this. I have five battle stars -- correction. I have five ribbons, and each ribbon has a Bronze Star for the five battles that we were in. I have a Bronze Star which was given to me, and this occurred at the Battle of the Bulge. They were coming fast, and it was a bridge that had to be blown, and Colonel Bailey, terrific colonel, wanted volunteers, and I and Sheriff -- Sheriff was a radio operator, a T3, and they came so fast we had to blow the bridge with the wrong end, and we did blow it, but we now were behind the lines. So I was MIA for -- well, Sheriff and I both, not just me. Those were the roughest days.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you MIA?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: About almost ten days, almost ten. I think the records show ten, but somehow it came about where we were approaching because we knew if we kept going north we would run into the British. This happened to be Queen Lace which is a Canadian outfit, and they challenged us. I can tell from the accent it was Canadian, and oh, boy, it was close. I had -- I was a master sergeant, so I did things before Sheriff did, not that he was afraid. He was gung-ho. He would have done it, but I did, and they thought we were Germans dressed like Americans, and so it was tough. They didn't take any bull or anything. And we finally go to an officer, and I asked if he would please get in touch with Apple, code name, 19th Corps. That's Apple, and yes -- and yeah, and Colonel Bailey recognized my voice right away, recognized who I was, and that I was okay, and he said he would be sending a Jeep for me, and let me talk to the officer, and so the two get together, and everything is fine. And sheriff and I finally get some clothes, some food, and we would rest and wait for the Jeep to come and pull us back into the outfit, but that was the closest I came to in my head of losing anything. The Rhine crossing. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else in the Bulge before you get to that?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Oh, the Bulge was -- again, we were lucky, and I'm going to take some food.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: We were lucky. When I say we were lucky, we were close enough to be in the fighting, but not close enough to have hand combat with the Germans coming through breaking through the lights, you know, so it always seemed -- it always seemed that there was an outfit of 29th that took a full rut, and they stopped them. We were right behind a 29, and we were there. So again, they are still laying lines to the battalions that were under us, so it wasn't easy. I mean, some of these guys would go out -- when I say some the these guys, the linemen would go out, and they had no idea if they were going to get back to us at that particular time, or whether if they were going to stay with a battalion and make it after things settled down a little bit because it was a combination of go, go, go, go, go, and then there would be a stop. And during this stop you would get things done, otherwise there just wasn't time, if I'm making myself clear. It's hard when you're not there to really depict what took place. It really is. But as I say, at the time of the Bulge, it was fearful. It was anticipation. We were still up there Heerlen, Holland when this thing started and everything stopped. And believe me, we were in almost a rest area. We were shaven. We had good clothes, things looked nice, and we were starting to live like a soldier would live, not anymore. And then all of a sudden this thing changed, and boy, off we went, supplies, ammunition. It was different, just like different from night and day. And as I say thanks, because of other soldiers and other organizations we were behind and not in front of. And even though we had to lay lines to some of the battalions that were up front, it would be laid, the lines, and then get back, you know. So it was -- it was a lot easier than it could be have been. The Bulge worked out, of course, in our favor, and no question. Patton did a good job when he got to them to relieve the pressure. Now, we had the right to cross, and Colonel Bailey said that what we we're going to do is we're going to have the 12th group get across the Rhine and setup communications from the other side of the Rhine backwards. Were going to do it this way. There's a reason for this, and he told us why because there were armored division that were going to be following us, that we were going to go in further and take the front and whatever is it out there. So we were one of the first troops to cross the lines, and we had an arrowhead. I forget the battle star, not a star. It's a ribbon, and with an arrow, that means that we were just like when we came in on D-Day, same thing is true. I have a star of an arrowhead. That's so I have the two arrowheads, one for the Rhine Crossing, one for the -- then we anticipated getting into Berlin, and they changed -- I mean, the orders came through, no. We were going to the Elg River, then we were going to meet the Russians. The Russians have now been given the permission by command or whatever to go in, and they are the ones that were going to occupy Berlin, so that is the first time that I met the Russians as a fighting force, and I was not impressed. I mean, it was a makeshift of thugs, of -- they weren't disciplined. They were not the same type of people that I was associated with as far as the U.S. Army was concerned. Completely different. They wanted to see our equipment. They looked it over carefully, and when we wanted to see their equipment, no. I mean, you just couldn't. It was an unusual situation; but anyway, that's the way it ended. The war ended. I remember giving the command, not I personally, but I mean, I wrote the massage out on the message blank that went to all the radio operators. "The wars has ended. Turn on your lights." That was it. "The war has ended. Turn on your lights." And then from there we went to the Elg River with the Russians, and then we went up straight north to Lauterbach where our assignment was to restore -- this is the 12th group now, to restore communications for the City of Lauterbach, and that's where we were. We completed that, and then we went down to Camp Lucky Strike. Oh, that's where the Ahken was disbanded. We ended up right there. And because I was a master sergeant, I was responsible for the equipment because you're talking thousands of dollars that had to be turned in to depots, various places, and then after that was assigned, assignment was completed, then I went down to Camp Lucky Strike, and I got on the Vina Victory landing ship LST, and that took us home. And end of report.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever see that girl again?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: No. I had telephone calls from her. I had telephone calls when she became a mother. We even -- my wife answered the phone and the conversation went something like this. "Was your husband in the services? Yes. Was he in Europe? Yes." There are a lot of Zimmermans. That's why this took place, and then the specific question, "Was he anywhere near the Albert Canal?" And we said yes, and then "What About Heerlen?" And then I heard her say, "We found him. We found him." And we talked on the phone, and she, by this time, had married, and it was just nice, nice to hear them and hear her voice. We've exchanged Christmas cards and correspondence along that line. I felt very close to her because of the experience of her father being underground and being killed, her mother, and she was a sweet lady, also being killed by the bombs that just dropped too short. And then she was taken over by her grandparents and raised by the grandparents, and I'm sure the Lord entered into this, and that was the best way to go rather than have her come into an Army organization, and I don't know what I would have done. I mean, she would have had to come forward to the states. I don't know how my wife would have handled it, you know. So many questions. Anyway, it worked out fine, but anyway, happy ending for her.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were married at the time?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Yes. Oh, yes. I married my high school bride. We were married 55 years. Marian died. And then Heidi -- Heidi is a twin. Her twin, Lynn, who lives out in San Diego, had a boy, and Marian and I were Godparents of that boy. That's how I knew Heidi. She also was Lutheran, and the things that she believes in I believe in. And she was wonderful. We have been married 10 years. It will be 11 years this November, so I had 55 years with my first wife, and now I have had 11 years with Heidi.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about mail call during the war. Did you get a lot of letters from your wife at all?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: No. No. Oh, boy, that was -- again, this is something that I never understood was, knowing Marian, I'm sure that she wrote many letters. I'm sure she did. Now, I got some, yes. I got some, but very few and in between. The reason I say that is we moved fast, and there were no post offices, you know, no post office. I know Heidi -- Marian has some of my FEmails back to her -- FEmail. FEmail, Femail, and that was -- I know I did not. No. No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No packages or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: No. No. In fact, I received no packages. Although, according to my dad -- and I was the only son -- he sent many things to me, but it just never caught up, no. What happened to them? I don't know. I just don't. That's a good question.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get any breaks, R and R breaks, anything like that?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Yes, in Holland. Now, this, remind you, we were in England, and we got no breaks in England, and France, we got no breaks in France. This continued on until we got into Holland. When I says things slowed down, and I had a chance to go to Paris, and that was wonderful. I mean, I was in Paris, I think, two days and I came back, and it was just wonderful. It was a wonderful experience for me, but that's the only break that I had. Then after the war, I'm now in Lauterbach. We were working on restoring communications for the City of Lauterbach. I forgot who the burger maestro was. But anyway -- oh, that was -- now, please, I'm a HAM radio operator. This place -- see, I volunteer at the VA Hospital in Brecksville, and we have a radio station and WBAA is our callers. We were talking to a lad from Texas -- I don't remember his call -- who just came back from Lauterbach, and he did not know me from Adam nor did I know him. And he astounded both Bill Nause (ph), who was on duty with me, by saying: "Behind the burger maestro's desk is a plaque, 'Thanks to the 12th group, Colonel Bailey commanding, for restoring communications.'" Oh, my ears dingled. I came back and I said, "Didn't you get a picture of that by chance?" Oh, I would have given anything for that, and he said, "No. I didn't take a picture of it." You know, and I never been to Lauterbach, and I would have loved to have seen that, you know. I really would have. But now, I mean, you're talking this transpired, oh, maybe five years ago Bill Naus, because I have been volunteering at the VA Hospital since '83, so anyway. That was something that I just threw in there because this came to my mind.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That brings us back to, were the German people pretty nice to you?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: You know, actually, I did not see the burger maestro, no. I'm sorry. In Lauterbach, yes, they respected us. They were nice to us. We stayed at a bombed out hotel, that was our headquarters, and the people were very nice to us. When I say they, they were very nice to us. I have to watch what I say.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not hostile?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: No. That's right. That's fine. That's a better word. They were not hostile to us. They didn't go out of their way to make me comfortable or anything like that, but at the same time they did listen to what I said. If I needed some help in doing this or that I would ask them, and they would do it. They were not antagonistic. I had no crazy Nazi-sort, so to speak. These were just normal Germans, I guess. I don't know. The people in France were frightened of what was going to happen to them. When I say that, the first night that we were there, we had the opportunity to see a husband and wife, and I believe it was a man or a young child, maybe a boy, and we wanted to help, and they absolutely -- now, I did not speak French, quite a few of the guys of my communications did, but they just wanted nothing to do with us. And at St. Lowell everything was destroyed. There were no -- I mean, the French would just go on, would just go on, so I did not encounter anyone that I could even hold any conversation with until I got to about Belgium, and that's when I ran into Watersand. He spoke English, broken English, but spoke fine, and he was the most cooperative, the most helpful from the underground, but that would be my only experience with the French. It just didn't workout. It just didn't seem to workout. That's all, and I didn't push it. Now, when I went on leave, I had R and R to Paris. I saw some -- I went to the luuv. I went to the luuv. I saw some shows. I went into cafe's there. It was a different story, but it was a different atmosphere completely because I don't know how else to say it. They knew that we were here to have some fun, and they wanted to help in any way, and so, it was good. Outside of that, no. I mean, I was very reserved as far as making friends. I wanted to get this thing over with and get home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Working our way backward, what was your impression of the people in England?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Oh, my. Oh, again, I had the pleasure of meeting fine men in England that were most receptive to the Americans being there, the Americans helping out. Reginald Fenwick is the gentleman I'm referring to now. He lost a son, spit fire pilot, who was killed. His daughter was with the communications section. This is why, I think, he liked me in England with the planes, and his wife had been killed, and he had been in World War II -- I, World War I, and was a home guard, but a fine gentleman, and we were able to speak intelligently. It was just wonderful. I mean, everyone that I had met that I recall that I had met in England treated me with respect and realized that it was a combination effort of beating the Nazis. The important thing was to beat the Nazis. And here, I should have offered this to you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, no, no. That's fine.

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: But, no, England was very good. I mean, I truly enjoyed the people in England.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What do you think about that time? Do any particular memories come to mind during those days?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Well, I can only say this, that this is when we took off. And when I say took off, we left Shetenburg (ph), I think, it was. I know I was near Baath Hedley (ph) on the teems, and then we took off for the staging area. And one of the last things that Reginald Fenwick did was give me a gold bracelet that had belonged to someone in the family and he said, "Take this and remember me," and he's dying, and he's dead. He was, as I say, World War I vintage, but -- and I never corresponded with the daughter. I just haven't. My own daughter, Bonnie Zimmerman, married an Englishman from Hartley Pool -- and because of the connection there by the north sea, he -- when I say he, is John, John Stevenson. John did some research when I was in England to see his dad, and they found out about Reginald Fenwick, and he was a barrister who had been retired and dead and buried now, but a well-known man and well-respected and so forth, and he was in World War I, so everything that he told me was true, and it's nice. It was nice. I mean, I guess that is why I keep referring to England as a nice place because of my son-in-law. I did meet his dad and his mother, and I remember vaguely, vaguely Hartley Pool, but I can't tell you why. All I know is on the north sea, and I know it's above London the way it is, but I somehow remember London -- not London, because I was at London. I mean, Hartley Pool, and I vaguely remember that, and I don't know how. I don't know why. That's about the story.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally did get back to the states?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Okay. Because I was master sergeant, I had to change and take all of the things to the depot. I was responsible for the equipment. The boys, when they were -- we were disbanded. They took off, and they got to Camp Lucky Strike before I did. It took me time to get this done, so I came back on LS -- no, a victory ship. I'm sorry. A victory ship, the Oneida Victory, and it was late in November, almost December, I think, and most of the boys had been back already. And so when I came in, I landed around 55th on a train, 55th and something, and I got ahold of a taxicab and came to 2047 East 96th Street where my wife was living in the apartment, and it was quiet. There was no fanfare. All the boys had come home, you know, and it was just wonderful to greet my wife. And then the following morning we went over to dad, and it was nice to get a hug from dad, and we went, I think, to the cemetery and viewed mother's grave, and then the rest of the family, oh, somehow appeared. We got together. It was wonderful. It was very, very nice. I remember that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That covers it?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: That's about it, yes. Thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: And, yeah. That shows when I got my --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: PFV, September '42, corporal, January '43, sergeant, February '43, staff sergeant, March '43, -- April '43, Master sergeant, June '43.

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Yeah, how about that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, went up to the ranks.

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. That General Omar Bradley is the one that presented me with the Bronze Star.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Got it directly from him?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I asked, did have you any other encounters with people like this, any conversations?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. The five star general by Eisenhower.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Dwight Eisenhower.

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. He was with us -- not with us. I'm sorry. He came got with Colonel Bailey. He didn't come down. It was sergeant, he was there. I remember the five stars on him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He didn't talk to you or anything? No?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: No. And if I'm not mistaken, I think I was on duty. I was operating a 610, a transmitter, and we were talking to -- headquarters or something. I don't remember. Well, I thank you for listening. Oh, I forgot to show and tell about Lady, honey. Lady, a little dachshund.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: A little dachshund in Ahken.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: In Ahken I had the pleasure of having a brown dachshund look at me. I called her. She bounded into my arms. I remember she was pregnant, and later on she had three puppies we called Acey, Ducey for our outfit, and then we thought that was the end of it, and then low and behold, Lucky appears. We had Acey, Ducey and Lucky, and they were with us for the remainder of the war. We gave them to engineers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you had mascots?

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Oh, absolutely. Absolutely, and they would bark. Oh, they would bark at the Germans, yeah. They would bark at the Germans.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Sheriff tried to put them in his duffle bag.

sp.speaker: Albert H. Zimmerman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But they wouldn't let him?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: No. They wouldn't let him.
